newsitem.title: UK: Hambros to be haunted by CWS debacle.
newsitem.headline: Hambros to be haunted by CWS debacle.

text.p: British merchant bank Hambros' humiliating climbdown over the failed hostile bid for the Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) will continue to haunt it for some time, analysts said on Wednesday.
"This will significantly affect Hambros' revenues from corporate advisory work for a year or so. It takes time for memories to fade," said one.
Hambros conceded on Monday it had been been wrong to support entrepreneur Andrew Regan's 1.2 billion pound ($2 billion) takeover attempt on the 153-year-old supermarkets-to-funeral parlours group.
Its chairman Sir Chips Keswick apologised unreservedly to CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth.

In addition to this and a "substantial" but confidential financial settlement, Hambros has also hired City law firm Norton Rose to conduct an investigation into why it supported a bid which was last week condemned by a London High Court judge.
The bank has given no detail on what the probe will involve or how long it is likely to take but it has informed the Bank of England and financial watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority (SFA).
Regan's bid for CWS was discredited by the revelation that confidential papers had been leaked by a senior CWS executive and had been passed on to the various parties involved, including Hambros.

But despite repeated calls by CWS chief Melmoth for Hambros to examine its role, the bank continued to back the break-up attempt, which was eventually scotched by CWS legal action and the withdrawal of funding by a key backer, to the bitter end.
Analysts differed in their assessment of just how damaging the affair would be to Hambros' overall business, with some suggesting the fallout would be limited to its corporate finance activities.
One said Hambros shares remained a buy because of the strong performance expected from its estate agency business Hambro Countrywide, which is benefitting from the recovery in the housing market.
"Hambro Countrywide will drive them forward."

But the CWS debacle will increase pressure from Hambros shareholders pushing for a break up of the bank to realise value. This has largely come from Hong Kong-based investment fund Regent Pacific group, which has a three percent holding in Hambros.

"The shares are largely being supported by the value argument," said the first analyst. Hambros shares were quoted at 238 pence at 0930 GMT but the analyst said they could be sold for between 300 and 340 pence a share in the event of a break-up.

Hambros is due to report its final results for the year to the end of March early in June. BZW analyst Robert Mumby forecasts pre-tax profits of 73.0 million pounds, up from 20.6 million pounds the previous year.
Hambros' banking business has struggled to perform in recent years and has been hit particularly by bad debt charges.

But the bank has maintained a reasonable mergers and acquisitions performance. In the 1996 league table of British public and private deals, compiled by Acquisitions Monthly magazine, Hambros ranked 7th with deals worth 7.8 billion pounds.
"They are still in there in the domestic corporate advisory markets. But this (the CWS affair) will make it difficult for them in 1997/1998," the first analyst said.
The bank could easily see clients jump ship, particularly if key corporate financiers are not cleared of any suggestion of not having acted corrrectly by the internal inquiry, he added.
And developing new clients will be made considerable harder by the bank's association with such a controversial and high profile bid.
Hambros has declined to comment on any aspect of the CWS bid beyond the statement it made on Monday.
($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
